segments.t: At the end of the day, Andrea brings the tax inspector Colette the papers she requested, including one document by mistake. After leaving the office, Andrea meets Gabriel outside the agency. He notices that the audit has unsettled her. Listen to the two conversations in French.
Je peux vous donner mes papiers?
Oui, bien sûr.
Voilà.
Madame Martel? Ça, ce n'est pas pour moi.
Ah bon? C'est quoi?
Ce sont vos résultats médicaux.
Oh, pardon! C'était sur mon bureau.
Au revoir, Madame Martel.
Oui, au revoir.
Tu es stressée par l'audit?
Tu n'aimes pas perdre le contrôle.
Tu es une femme de pouvoir, Andréa!
On va manger?
Non, je rentre chez moi.
Merci quand même.
Tu as raison. À demain.
Let's go through it. Andréa walks up to Colette's desk with a pile of documents, being extra polite.
Je peux vous donner mes papiers?
'Can I give you my papers?' Andréa uses the formal 'you' with Colette. The formal 'you' sits between 'can' and 'give', because it means 'to you'.
Oui, bien sûr.
'Yes, of course.' Polite, but not warm. Colette is all business.
Voilà.
'There you go.' The word you say as you hand something over.
Madame Martel? Ça, ce n'est pas pour moi.
'Ms Martel? This isn't for me.' Colette has found something in the pile that shouldn't be there.
Ah bon? C'est quoi?
'Really? What is it?' The first two words show surprise, a little like 'oh, really?'. The question 'what is it' puts the question word at the end, as people often do when speaking.
Ce sont vos résultats médicaux.
'It's your medical results.' Oops. A very private document has slipped in with the tax papers. The verb is the plural form, because 'results' is plural.
Oh, pardon! C'était sur mon bureau.
'Oh, sorry! It was on my desk.' The second word is a quick 'sorry'.
Au revoir, Madame Martel.
'Goodbye, Ms Martel.' Very correct, with the title and the surname.
Oui, au revoir.
'Yes, goodbye.' The farewell ends Andrea's embarrassed exchange with Colette. Later, outside the agency, Gabriel notices that Andrea is unsettled.
Tu es stressée par l'audit?
'Are you stressed about the audit?' Gabriel uses the familiar form of 'you' with his colleague Andrea. That differs from the polite form she used with the inspector inside.
Tu n'aimes pas perdre le contrôle.
'You don't like losing control.' The familiar word for 'you' comes before the negative. The basic action 'lose' follows 'like', without the English ending in 'ing'.
Tu es une femme de pouvoir, Andréa!
'You're a woman who likes power, Andrea!' Literally 'a woman of power'. Gabriel suggests that her discomfort comes from facing something she cannot control.
On va manger?
'Shall we go and eat?' The everyday word for 'we' comes before 'go' and then the plain action 'eat'. Gabriel offers to continue the evening over a meal.
Non, je rentre chez moi.
'No, I'm going home.' French says 'I return to my place'. The final words locate the return at the speaker's home. Andrea declines the invitation.
Merci quand même.
'Thanks anyway.' The last two words mean 'all the same' or 'anyway'. Andrea acknowledges Gabriel's invitation while keeping her answer a clear no.
Tu as raison. À demain.

'You're right. See you tomorrow.' French says 'have reason' where English says 'be right'. Gabriel uses the familiar form with Andrea and accepts her decision to go home. Now let's listen to the whole scene one more time.
Je peux vous donner mes papiers?
Oui, bien sûr.
Voilà.
Madame Martel? Ça, ce n'est pas pour moi.
Ah bon? C'est quoi?
Ce sont vos résultats médicaux.
Oh, pardon! C'était sur mon bureau.
Au revoir, Madame Martel.
Oui, au revoir.
Tu es stressée par l'audit?
Tu n'aimes pas perdre le contrôle.
Tu es une femme de pouvoir, Andréa!
On va manger?
Non, je rentre chez moi.
Merci quand même.
Tu as raison. À demain.

An embarrassing document ends Andrea's conversation with Colette. Outside, Gabriel offers a little company, but Andrea chooses to go home. You have heard how to hand something over, apologise and decline an invitation politely. See you next time!
Bonne soirée!
